Annexure XIII to Loan Policy 
Guidelines on Pre-Sanctioned Credit Lines through 
Unified Payments Interface 
1. Introduction 
 
1.1 In the monetary policy meeting dated 06.04.2023 , the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)  has 
approved the operation of pre-sanctioned credit lines at Banks through Unified Paymen t 
Interface (UPI). This facility assists the citizens to avail and utilize the low ticket but 
high-volume retail loans that will boost the consumption and livelihood in the country.  
 
1.2 A Pre-sanctioned credit line on Unified Payment Interface (UPI) allows th e individual to 
access the pre-approved credit, with prior consent, directly through UPI platform thereby 
enabling seamless transactions and immediate access to funds. The credit line is  linked 
to the individual’s UPI ID and can be  used as a funding account.  In other words, a credit 
line is a type of loan that provides the customer with a predetermined am ount of money 
that can be access ed any time with the facility to withdraw funds multiple times as 
needed. Unlike traditional personal loans, where the customer receives a lump sum 
upfront and repay it over time, a credit line allows to withdraw funds whenever 
required, up to the approved limit. 
 
2. Regulatory Guidelines  
 
2.1 Reserve Bank of India vide their notification no: RBI/2023- 24/58 CO.DPSS.POLC.No.S-
567/02-23-001/2023-2024 dated 04.09.2023 has expand ed the scope of UPI by enabling 
transfer to/from pre-sanctioned credit line at bank s. RBI in its notification has specified 
that Banks may, as per their Board approved policy, stipulate terms and conditio ns for 
use of Pre-Sanctioned credit lines. The terms may include among other items, credit  
limit, period of credit, rate of interest etc.  
 
2.2 Further, National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has communicated the guid elines 
on Credit L ine through UPI vide th eir operating circular number NPCI/UPI/OC No: 
171/2023-24 dt 20.09.2023 covering all the operational points to be followed.  
 
3. Credit Line on UPI 
 
3.1 Currently Savings account, Overdraft account, prepaid wallets and RuPay Credit Ca rds 
can be linked to UPI. With the introduction of Credit line on UPI, users will be able to add 
pre-sanctioned credit lines issued by the Bank for transactions through the UPI System. 
The key design principles for credit line on UPI are as follows:

PAGE 315
Loan Policy   
 
          Page 281 of 282 
 
i. It is a pre-sanctioned credit line to an individual with prior consent to enable  
transactions using the UPI system.  
ii. Transactions will work on the UPI market infrastructure as per UPI procedural 
guidelines.  
iii. Transaction will be authenticated using UPI authentication mechanisms.  
iv. Amount will be debited real time from customer’s Credit account through UPI.  
v. UPI settlement process will be followed, NPCI will provide separate Org Id, and  hence 
separate settlement reports will be provided to the UPI Credit issuers.  
 
3.2 It is an innovative financial offering designed to revolutionize the lending landscape. This 
facility shall empower individuals to access pre-sanctioned credit lines from lenders. It 
facilitates the availability of low-ticket, high-volume retail loans, fostering economic 
growth and enhancing financial inclusion.  For credit line products (like KCC, SOD-FDR 
etc.), customer will use UPI as an additional channel to enable the payment through the 
credit line linked accounts. 
 
3.3 This shall provide a seamless, UPI enabled credit lifestyle experience to the customers. 
Customers shall benefit from the ease and the increased opportunity to use their credit 
lines. Merchant shall benefit from the increase in consumption by being part of credit 
ecosystem with acceptance of credit lines using QR codes and other pay ment acceptance 
methods. UPI has become the most preferred payment method in the recent times.  
Enablement of Credit line through UPI may have huge potential for the growth of the  
credit portfolio of the Bank. Linking of credit line on UPI will provide an a ssurance to the 
customer for safe and secure transactions. 
 
4. Objective 
 
The objective of Credit Line is to provide additional channel to the customer t o utilize 
the related merchant payments through UPI in a safe, secure and faster way. Credit li ne 
is an extension of the credit card to facilitate payment through running loan ac counts or 
other credit line products. 
 
5. Scope 
 
The scope of pre-sanctioned credit line is given below:  
i. Discovery and linking of Credit Line accounts 
ii. Setting UPI PIN through Debit Card (if applicable) or Aadhaar +OTP 
iii. Transaction Processing 
iv. Settlement and Reconciliation 
v. Dispute Management 
 
6. Features of the Product 
 
6.1 Seamless Linking: Based on the registered mobile number, individuals can link credit line 
on UPI using their Aadhaar Authentication or debit card issued to the credi t facility. 
Further, two factor authentications can also be allowed for linking of credit  line. Only 
Pre-Sanctioned Credit Lines (revolving/ non-revolving) can be linked to UPI.

PAGE 316
Loan Policy   
 
          Page 282 of 282 
 
6.2 Secure Authentication: The payment transactions can be authenticated with a 
dedicated UPI PIN for Credit Line on UPI, enhancing security and preventing unauthorized 
access. 
 
6.3 Credit Line Details: Customer can get comprehensive insights on Credit line such as 
status, utilized amount, due amount details etc. directly within the UPI app. 
 
6.4 Transaction Variety: The borrower can make the payment only to merchants QR Codes,             
e-comm merchants using Credit line on UPI. No peer to peer (P2P) transactions  are 
allowed to ensure end use of funds. 
6.5 Transaction Limits: Standard UPI transaction limits shall be applicable. Limits of Credit 
line on UPI transactions shall be similar to existing UPI transaction limits. 
 
6.6 Repayment Methods: To utilize repayment methods effectively, including inward 
payments to the specific UPI ID for credit line repayment, and utilize e-ma ndates 
(AutoPay), wherever applicable. 
 
6.7 Online Dispute Resolution: The disputes can be resolved conveniently through UDIR 
(Uniform Dispute and Issue Resolution) feature available in UPI Apps. 
 
7. Grievance Redressal Mechanism 
 
7.1 Any customer having grievances can raise the same through CRM portal by selecting 
appropriate department based on the grievance type. The respective department sh all 
view the grievance and provide appropriate solution within the TAT defined by the bank. 
 
7.2 Customer can choose the verticals based on grievance type which are broadly defined a s 
under: 
 
i. For Credit line on UPI transaction issues: 
 
UPI Claims team in Recon Vertical - For financial claims, chargebacks, disputes etc . of 
UPI transactions initiated through Credit line. 
 
UPI team in Digitization Vertical - For UPI issues such as unable to link the account, set 
UPI PIN, unable to perform transaction etc. 
 
ii. For any other product/credit related issues: 
 
Respective credit owner vertical - For any other product/credit related disputes. 
 
The other operational aspects such as process flow for UPI credit line set- up, financial 
transaction, eligibility criteria, transaction limits etc are separately defined in the 
operational guidelines to pre-sanctioned credit lines on Unified Payment Interface (UPI).

1. POLICY OVERVIEW 
                                                                                                                                                                           
1.1 PREAMBLE 
 
1.1.1  Indian Banking system has played a crucial role in the socio-economic development of the 
country. The system is expected to continue to be sensitive to the growth a nd 
development needs of all the segments of the society. Extending credit is a  basic 
function of banking which involves risks. The Bank should aim at managing risk in such a 
way that a healthy credit portfolio is built and returns are maximized. 
 
1.1.2 The Reserve Bank of India comes out with guidelines on management of credi t risk from 
time to time and fine tune the existing risk management systems, to face the emerging  
challenges in the fast-changing environment and to undertake robust credit risk 
management functions in a more responsive and proactive manner. In the a bove 
backdrop, the Bank has upgraded its credit risk policy covering activities where credit 
risk is assumed.   
 
1.1.3 The Loan Policy of the Bank has in-built flexibilities to meet the challenges in the market 
place. The Policy, at the holistic level, is an embodiment of the Bank' s approach to 
sanctioning, managing, and monitoring credit risk and aims at making the system s and 
controls effective.  
 
1.1.4 Circulars: Instruction/Information circulars issued from time to time include detailed 
operating framework, which shall be in consonance with the Loan Policy of the Bank . In 
case of any contradiction, the guidelines of the Loan Policy shall prevail over a ny of the 
earlier circulars issued by the Bank. 
 
1.1.5 Manual of Advance: Manual of Advances of Bank in electronic form is available in UBINET 
and updated by Union Bank Knowledge Center (UBKC)/ Union Learning Academy Staff 
Training College/ Center (STC), Bengaluru. The manual shall be updated by Union 
Learning Academies (ULA) on Half-yearly basis. 
 
1.1.6 Operational Guidelines : Various operational Guidelines hitherto enumerated in Loan 
Policy are now separately issued as ‘Operational guidelines to Policy’ . Credit Risk 
Management Committee (CRMC) is empowered for modificati on in operational guidelines 
to the policy.  
 
1.1.7 The Loan Policy is reviewed every year to keep in sync with the market realities, business 
priorities, Government policies and regulatory requirements. The Loan Policy is being 
reviewed / fine-tuned in line with the developments in the financial sector, Regula tory 
and Government Policies, while keeping intact its basic tenets. This updated version of

1.2 OBJECTIVES: 
   
  The Basic Tenets of the Loan Policy are mentioned as under: 
 
1.2.1 The Loan Policy applies to Domestic Lending. For Foreign Branches we have separate 
policies which have been framed by Domestic Foreign Business & International Banking 
Department (DFB&IBD) taking into account the banking and other regulatio ns of the host 
country on one hand and the Govt of India/Reserve Bank of India guidelines /regulatio n 
on the other hand.  
 
1.2.2 The policy seeks to enlarge client base of Corporate and Non-Corporate segments through 
aggressive Credit Marketing. 
 
1.2.3 To addresses the genuine credit needs of the existing clients by ensuring quicker an d 
prompt credit decision. 
 
1.2.4 To establish a commonality of approach regarding credit basics, appraisal skills and 
strategies, while leaving enough room for flexibility and innovation.  
 
1.2.5 The policy aims to seize market opportunities by revamping our products and delivery 
mechanism through product innovation and restructuring with a view to maximize 
profits. 
 
1.2.6 The policy strives to ensure that the socio-economic obligations cast on the Ba nk are 
fully met.  
 
1.2.7 The Policy seeks to ensure continuous growth of loan assets while endeavoring that they 
remain secure, performing and standard.  
 
1.2.8 The Policy endeavors to mitigate and reduce risk associated with the lending by  fine 
tuning the Systems and Controls.  
 
1.2.9 The Policy recognizes and accords due priority to Computerization, Lending Autom ation 
Solution (LAS), Management Information Systems (MIS) based on a reliable database and 
development of faster communication as tools for better overall Credit Risk Management.  
 
1.2.10 The Policy lays down take-over norms for advances from other Banks / FIs. 
 
1.2.11 The Policy seeks to ensure profitable deployment of resources keeping in view the Asset 
Liability Management (ALM) requirements.

1.2.12 The Policy document ensures compliance of the directives / guidelines issued by 
Government/RBI and other regulatory requirements on credit matters. With regard to

their aspects. However, if these permit varying interpretations, the Bank will  adopt a

1.3 SCOPE 
  
1.3.1 This Policy covers aspects of Credit Appraisal, Sanction and Disbursement for credit 
related exposures; Fund Based as well as Non-Fund based and has prescribed acceptance 
criteria for various forms of Credit Dispensation. These would include Short Term, 
Medium Term and Long Term based facilities, as also Letters of Credit, Guarant ees, 
Acceptances, Derivatives, Forward Contracts, Underwriting the Loans etc.  
 
1.3.2 The Investment policy of the Bank has been framed separately, which covers various 
aspects of the Bank’s Treasury and Investment functions. For post -disbursement 
monitoring, a separate Credit Monitoring Policy is in place. Further, Risk Manage ment 
Department has framed a separate “Credit Risk Man agement Policy” outlining the entire 
gamut of risks perceived and their mitigations. 
 
1.3.3 The Policy encompasses exposure to various types of customers such as Individ uals, 
Proprietorship Firms, Partnerships, Association of Persons, Companies registered under 
the Indian Companies Act, Undertakings owned by the Government, Limited Liability  
Partnerships (LLPs), Trusts, Societies and others. 
 
1.3.4 This policy has been made in compliance with all RBI and extant regulatory gu idelines 
issued till date. The guidelines enumerated in the policy are applicable for all  domestic 
operations. 
 
1.4 Verticals at Central Office: Credit functions are divided into the following verticals: 
 
1.4.1 Agri Business Department (ABD)  – Focus on growth in Agriculture through Agriculture 
Loan Points (ALPs) and other agriculture branches.  
 
1.4.2 Retail Assets Vertical  – Focus on growth in Retail Lending Schemes through Retail Loan 
Point (RLP) and other branches. 
 
1.4.3 Large Corporate Vertical (LCV) – LCV shall focus on wholesale advances growth through 
Large Corporate Branches (LCBs).  
 
1.4.4 MSME – MSME will oversee credit related functions including formulation of credit related 
products except Retail and Agriculture for domestic operations, focus on growt h of 
advance under MSME through MSME Loan Points (ML Ps) / Union MSME First Branches 
(UMFBs) & Other Branches (Except MCBs & LCBs).

4.6 Borrower Standards 
 
4.6.1 Financial Strength 
 
4.6.1.1 The financial strength of the borrower client shall be considered adequate, in relation to 
the project size/volume of operations proposed to be undertaken and risks involved 
therein in the light of acceptable parameters. The methodology for co mputation of net 
worth / means for different type of borrowers is issued through a separate circular. 
 
4.6.1.2 In depth analysis of Audited Profit & Loss Statement shall be done and deta iled 
comparative comments on EBIDTA Margins, cash flows from Operation (Actual & 
Projected) and other parameters as per financial Break-up , whichever is applicable shall 
be captured in the Executive Summary. 
 
4.6.1.3 Sensitivity Test: 
 
Branches / Offices should carry out sensitivity tests/scenario analysis while sanct ioning 
Term Loan for la rge projects (with credit limits of Rs.10 crore and above: i ncluding 
existing Term Loan exposure), especially for infrastructure projects, which should inter  
alia include project delays and cost overruns. This will aid in taking a vi ew on viability of 
the project at the time of deciding Corrective Action Plan (CAP). 
 
Further, parameters of sensitivity test shall be decided based on nature of business  
activity, estimation of probability of variation etc. 
 
4.6.1.4 Quality of Capital: 
 
Branches / Offices should ascertain the source and quality of equity capital brought in by 
the promoters /shareholders. Multiple leveraging, especially, in infrastructure projects, 
is a matter of concern as it effectively camouflages the financial ratios such as 
Debt/Equity ratio, leading to adverse selection of the borrowers. Therefore, it shoul d be 
ensured at the time of credit appraisal that debt of the parent company is not infused as 
equity capital of the subsidiary/SPV. 
 
4.6.1.5 Margin and security stipulations shall not act as a substitute for due dilig ence on credit 
worthiness of the borrower.

4.6.2.9 Internal Rate of Return (IRR - Project): 
 
4.6.2.9.1 IRR is the discount rate which makes the Net Present Value ( NPV) of future cas h flows

its IRR should be greater than the weighted average cost of capital.

within the banking system. There are two types of Participations Inter-Bank 
Participations with Risk Sharing; and Inter-Bank Participations without Risk Sharing. 
a. Inter-Bank Participations with Risk Sharing: The primary objective of the Pa rticipations is 
to provide some degree of flexibility in the credit portfolio of banks and to  smoothen the 
working of consortium arrangements. 
 
➢ Period of Participations - The minimum period of such Participation will be 91 days, 
while the maximum period will be 180 days. 
➢ Selection of Accounts - Banks shall participate only in respect of advances/po rtfolio 
consisting of investment grade borrowers i.e. rated BBB and above. Th e aggregate 
amount of such Participations in any account should not exceed 40 per cen t of the 
outstanding in the account at the time of issue. During the currency of the 
Participations the aggregate amount of Participations should be covered by the 
outstanding balance in the account. In case the outstanding balance falls short of the 
participations outstanding, the issuing bank will reduce the Participations t o the 
extent necessary and if need be, issue Participations for smaller amounts. 
➢ Risk - The risk would be deemed to have crystallised when the issuing bank recalls the 
advances and stops operations in the relative account. In such a case the issuing bank 
would give due notice to the participating bank intimating the default.

10.1 The concept of Group and the task of identification of the borrowers belonging to 
specific industrial groups have been left to the perception of Banks by Reserve Ba nk of

10.2 Two or more enterprises is said to belong to the same group, if at any time during the 
reporting period or during the period under review, the financial or operati ng decisions 
of the said enterprises a re “Controlled” or “persons acting in concert” or “significantly 
influenced” by the same enterprises / persons. The words controlle d and persons acting 
in concert will have the meaning as defined in SEBI (Substantial A cquisition of shares and 
Takeovers) Regulation, 1997 as amended and modified from time to time and shall be 
construed accordingly. In simple layman language, if at any time du ring the reporting 
period or during the period under review, a person / enterprise has a say in the day- to-
day management of the other firm, then the two entities will be considered as a part of 
same group. For e.g. In the process of Due Diligence if it is r evealed that A of ABC Ltd is 
actively involved or is in a p osition to influence decision making in XYZ Ltd, then both 
will be deemed to be Group Companies. 
 
The detailed guidelines on group approach are covered in Operational guidelines to loan 
policy.

15. Structured Mezzanine Debt Facility: 
 
15.1 Infrastructure sect or is characterized by long gestation periods and large capex 
requirements. Non-recourse funding therefore becomes a pre-dominant product in this 
market. India is in the midst of a major infrast ructure investment boom and there exists a 
huge appetite for w ell-structured debt products and mezzanine debt products, which 
support specific project activities (pre-development funding or take out funding  for 
implementation period) or have a linkage to r eturns profile (mezzanine products) or 
enhance the credit for senior lenders (liquidity support, subordinated debt).  
 
15.2 Traditionally, the funding of capacity creation in India has been through Development 
Financial Institutions and more recently through ba nks and public issues. There has been an 
increase in credit off take and corporate loans have witnessed high growth. 
 
15.3 Traditionally Corporate borrowers have been financed on the basis of strength or weakness 
of balance sheet, with the credit quality of the borrower being the single m ost important 
factor. But of late the borrowings are being closely linked to the value of the asset or the  
revenue earning capability of the assets – by means of structured finance. With this 
background, a need was felt for innovative ways of funding to the corporates and Structured 
Mezzanine Debt Facility (SMDF) is one such innovation. 
  
15.4 The Structured Mezzanine Debt Facility (SMDF) is being established primarily to provide 
mezzanine funding to Indian Companies to enable them to scale up their si ze of operations 
by ex ploiting opportunities in the current phase of growth in the Indian economy . These 
opportunities span across multiple sectors as well as local and international horizons.  
 
15.5 The Bank shall participate in structured lo an facility such as Mezzanine Credit fac ilities to

master direction no. DBR.FSD.No.101/24.01041/2015-16 dated 25.09.2017. In terms of RBI 
guidelines, the business of factoring should be undertaken in compliance with the statutory

22.1.2 The Factoring Regulation Act, 2011 defines ‘factoring business’ as business of acquisition of 
receivables of assignor by accepting assignment of such receivables or financing, whether by

way of making loans or advances or otherwise against the security inter est over any

ii. any activity as commission agent or otherwise for sale of agricultural produce or goods of 
any kind whatsoever or any activity relating to the production, storage, supply, distribution, 
acquisition or control of such produce or goods or provision of any services. 
The terms assignee, assignor and debtor will have the same meaning as assigned to them in 
the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011 viz., 
 
"Assignee" means a factor in whose favour the receivable is transferred; 
"Assignor" means any person who is the owner of any receivable; and 
"Debtor" means any person liable to the assignor, whether under a contract  or otherwise, to 
pay any receivable or discharge any obligation in respect of the receivable whether existing, 
accruing, future, conditional or contingent. 
 
22.2 RBI in its notification has stated that Banks may formulate a comprehensive fac toring

master direction dated 26.05.2016 (updated as on 25.09.2017) states the below aspects: 
  
22.2.1 Factoring Business through a Subsidiary:  
 
In terms of regulatory norms, a Bank intending to form a subsidiary for undertaking 
factoring business shall be subject to the conditions specifie d in section 5, chapter II of 
Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Financial Services provided by Banks) Directions, 
2016 dated 26.05.2016 (updated 25.09.2017). 
 
22.2.2 Factoring business departmentally:  
 
Factoring business undertaken departmentally shall be subject to the following conditions: 
 
i. Factoring services shall be provided on with recourse or without recou rse or on limited 
recourse basis.  
 
ii. All underwriting c ommitments pertaining to the credit risk on the debtor, under withou t 
recourse factoring, shall be in accordance with the Board approved limits.  
 
iii. A thorough credit appraisal of the debtors shall be carried out by banks before entering into 
any factoring arrangement or establishing lines of credit with the export factor.

SECTION –I  
1. Background  
Collateral Management is one of the important tools in Credit Risk Management. Collaterals 
mitigate the risk of borrower’s default and also is a comfort f or the lender, if the borrower 
defaults. As loans an d advances constitute significant por tion of Ban k’s bal ance sheet, 
management of collaterals are inevitable for ensuring survival and success of the Bank. 
 
2. Objectives of the Policy 
2.1. To serve as guideline for management of prime and collateral security acce pted / proposed 
to be accepted by the Bank, against an e xisting / proposed expos ure, so that Bank’s 
interests, rights and capital are protected. 
2.2. To serve as guidelines for addressing and mitigating various risks includi ng Credit Risk and 
Residual risks arising out of primary and collateral security accepted by the Bank. 
2.3. To serve as th e guidelines for Credit Risk Mitigation Techniques in the Bank as per 
regulatory guidelines and Internal Policies for risk management. 
 
3. Scope of the Guidelines 
The guidelines on Collateral Management of the Bank wi ll be applicable to all business lines 
and units of the Bank, in respect of exposures in the ‘Banking Book’ by way of loans and 
advances. The collateral management of the exposures covered in the Trading Book  and 
investment exposures shall be covered by the Treasury Policy of the Bank.

of the guidelines. 
 
4.2. The Credit verticals in the Bank and the various sanctioning authorities h ave to ensure 
implementation and complianc e with this guideline in their functioning and decision 
making. Whenever collateral related policies of credit products (new / existing) a re to be 
approved/ modified, the credit verticals shall place the same before CRMC for deliberations 
and approval. The recommendations of CRMC shall be implemented by the Credit Verticals  
and compliance shall be placed before CRMC / RMC for information. Risk Management

periodical review, as and when required.

SECTION –III 
 
MANAGEMENT OF RESIDUAL RISKS IN COLLATERIZATION 
 
1. Although the Bank derives benefit out of Collateral Management System, there are 
number of Residual Risks that arise from the proce ss.  Residual risks include legal, 
operational, li quidity and market risks. Therefore, it is impera tive that banks employ 
robust procedures and processes to control these risks, including strategy; consideration 
of the underlying credit; valuation; policie s and procedures; systems; control of roll-off 
risks; and management of concentration risk arising from the bank’s use of C RM 
techniques and its interaction with the bank’s overall credit risk profile. As per Pillar-2 
guidelines, RBI undertakes Supervisory review process of the bank wherein bank’s control 
and mitigation process of residual risks are ass essed. If these risks ar e not adequately 
controlled, Reserve Bank may decide to impose additional capital charges or  take other 
supervisory actions. 
 
2. The bank may face the following sources of risk for Collateralizing Transaction: 
 
2.1. Operational Risk: 
 
2.1.1. Collateral Agreement Structur ing requires special knowledge/skills to avoid creating/ 
documenting agreements that are operationally burdensome or legally ineffective.  
 
2.1.2. Prescribing of standardized documentation for each product/ or type of collateral as well 
as vetting by the legal de partment for non-standardized documents to check accuracy 
and adequacy will minimize operational errors. Similarly, up-dation of docu ments has to 
be made on enhancement, modification etc. of facilities and also as per provisions of Law 
of limitation / docu mentation policy of the Bank. Branches and authorized persons 
executing the documents have to exercise utmost care in ensuring accura cy, adequacy 
and timeliness of the documents.  
 
2.1.3. Collateral Monitoring, if not done on a regular basis, with accurate data & reporting, may 
give rise to a risk of value of the collaterals getting reduced or depleted or  become 
unenforceable. 
 
2.2. Market Risk 
 
2.2.1. Arises due to decrease/ fluctuation in market value of collaterals. Haircuts/ m argins are 
prescribed to minimize the risks of value of collaterals falling below the credit exposure 
even in situations of extreme volatility. 
 
2.2.2. If the actual price volatility of the asset is not back-tested from time to time versus th e 
haircuts applied, then there is a potential for loss situation to increase.

2.2.3. A regular review of market risk and asset haircuts is the prudent minimum and for mo re 
volatile and less liquid assets a more frequent review is to be done. 
 
2.2.4. An inbuilt mec hanism to increase collection of securities/ marg in in case of highly 
volatile securities like shares, base metals, gold etc will minimize the risk. 
 
2.2.5. To assess the impact of market risk, Risk Management Dep artment also conducts stres s 
testing in case of ho using loans. As per the stress testing policy, th e scenario of fall in 
housing prices and subsequent increase in Loan to Value ratio is assessed on a quarterly 
basis to estimate the impact on CRAR and the results are reported to CRMC and RMC. 
 
2.3. Risk of loss of physical collaterals due to casualty events 
 
2.3.1. In case of physical coll aterals such as stock of goods, machinery, building, land, vehicles 
etc., there is a risk of loss of such collaterals due to causalit y events such as theft , 
pilferage, fire, earthquake, acc idents, flood and certain manmade disasters like acts of 
terrorism. The branches shall ensure that securities charged to the Bank, shall be 
adequately insured against such plausible events, with the n ame of Bank as loss payee. 
Branches shall also ensure that the cover is adequate in relation to the va lue of security 
and e xposure amount due to the Bank. The cost of insurance shall be borne by the 
Borrower. Branches shall also ensure that the insurance p olicies are kept up to date in 
the records to avoid the risk of non-coverage. 
 
2.3.2. National Disaster Ma nagement Guidelines on E nsuring Disaster Resilient construction of

2.3.2.1. Bank has to ensure that physical assets created through loa ns rem ain safe and 
disaster resilient. Hence, the guidelines prepared by NDMA can be adopted by the

extensions or alteration of houses financed. Further, depending on the na ture o f 
the asset and the vulnerability of the location to any of the disasters, the  bank 
could insist on ensuring that the disaster resistant features of NDMA guidelines are

bank’s approved valuer/architect sh ould certify that the construction is compliant

or same locatio n.  In such a situation, the enforcement may become difficult ,

2.5. Correlation Risk 
2.5.1. Correlation risk arises w hen a borrower/third party delivered collateral assets are 
highly/adversely correlated to borrower’s credit  performance/quality itsel f. Eg: 
Obtaining guarantee from parent company whose cre dit worthiness/ value is dependent 
on the b orrower, obtaining secur ity of a company whose cash flows depends on the 
borrower. Hence, the credit quality of the counter-party and the value o f the collateral 
should not have material positive co-relation. Corr elation may be reduced or eliminated 
by careful choice of collateral assets.    
 
2.5.2. As per RBI’s NCAF guidelines, for collateral to provide protection, the credit quality of 
the counterparty and the valu e of the collateral must not have a material positive 
correlation. For example, securities issued b y the counterparty - or by any related group 
entity - would provide little protection and so would be ineligible for CRM for c omputing 
regulatory capital.

not have any material correlation with the business cycle of the same borrower

SECTION-IV 
 
Part A: Credit Risk Mitigation Techniques as per Basel- guidelines (Standardized   Approach)  
  
1. Currently Our Bank is following the Basel- II ‘Standardized Approach’ for Credit Risk as 
per the RBI’s Basel -II guidelines on New Capital Adequacy Framework (NCAF). Bank shall 
accept all types of securities based on acceptance criteria for credi t decisions. For 
capital adequacy purposes, Bank shall reckon only a few categori es of “Elig ible 
Collaterals” as prescribed  by RBI Master Circular on NCAF (New Capital Adequacy 
Framework), July, 2015. 
 
2. The New Capital Accord of Basel has proposed the follo wing credit risk mitigation 
techniques for computation of net exposure for capital adequacy purposes. Banks have to 
calculate their ‘Adjusted exposure’ to a counterparty for capital adequacy purposes to 
take account of the effects of underlying collateral. 
 
Adjusted Value of Exposure = Gross Exposure - Net Value of 
eligible collaterals after haircuts. 
 
2.1. Thus, Credit Risk Mitig ation refers to reduction permitted in overall exposure (credit-
FB/NFB/ Investment) to a counterparty by offsetting the exposure with the following 
items:- 
 
2.1.1. Collateralized transactions. 
2.1.2.  Treatment of Guarantees 
2.1.3.  On Balance-sheet netting 
 
2.2. While the use of C RM techniques reduces or transfers credit risk, it simultaneously may 
increase other risks (residual risks). The Management of such risks is covered in Section III.

6. Approaches for CRM Techniques. 
 
6.1. The revised framework allows banks to adopt either A) The Simple Approach or B) The 
Comprehensive Approach while recognizing eligible financial collaterals. 
 
6.2. RBI has permitted Indian banks to adopt only Comprehensive Approach. In tune w ith the 
RBI directions, Bank shall adopt the Comprehensive Approach. 
 
6.3. Comprehensive Approach allows fuller offset of haircut adjusted collateral value agains t 
exposures, by effectively reducing the exposure amount by the haircut-adjusted value of 
collaterals. 
 
6.4. Under this approach , bank, which take eligible financial collaterals (e.g., cash or 
securities, more specifically defined in this policy), is allowed to reduce the credit 
exposure (FB+NFB) to counterparty when calculating capital requirements to ta ke 
account of the risk mitigating effect of the collateral.  
 
6.5. Credit risk mitigation is allowed only on an account- by-account basis, even within 
regulatory retail portfolio. 
 
7. Haircuts 
 
7.1. Banks are required to adjust both the amount of the exposure to the counter-pa rty and 
the value of any collateral received in support of that counter-party to take account of 
possible future fluctuations in the value of either, due to market movements.  Thes e 
adjustments are referred to as “haircuts”.    
 
7.2. The application of hair cuts will produce volati lity-adjusted amounts for both exposure 
and collateral.  
 
7.2.1. The ‘haircut’ for the exposure will be a premium factor and the ‘haircut’ f or the 
collateral will be a discount factor. 
 
7.2.2. Haircuts shall be applied to all counterparties where the bank desires to ava il of credit 
risk mitigation benefits and shall be determined by the maturity of the exposure, 
external rating assigned to the exposure and counterparty category. 
 
7.2.3. Bank shall apply appropriate haircut as per RBI final guidelines for ad justing collateral 
value and exposure.  
 
7.3. In principle, banks have two ways of calculating the haircuts :- 
7.3.1. Standard Supervisory haircuts. 
7.3.2. Own Estimate haircuts, using Bank’s own internal estimates of market price volatility.

7.3.3. Banks in India are permitted to use only the Standard Supervisory Haircuts and the 
haircut for exposure and collateral as per RBI final guidelines on NCAF are deta iled in 
Appendix – 1. 
 
7.3.4. The value of credit exposures acquired by banks in banki ng operations, would not be 
subject to mark et volatility, (since th e loan disbursal / investment would be a “cash” 
transaction). Only the value of eligible financial collateral would be subject to the 
haircut stipulated in Appendix-1 in respect of credit transactions only but not to the 
credit exposure of the bank. 
 
7.3.5. On th e other hand, exposures of banks, arising out of repo-style transactions would 
require upward adjustment for volatility, as the value of security sold/lent /pledged in 
the repo transaction, would be subject to market volatility. Henc e, such exposures shall 
attract haircut. 
 
8. Maturity mismatch  
 
8.1. If the residual maturity of the CRM is less than that of the underlying credit expo sure, a 
maturity m ismatch occurs. Where there is a maturity mismatch and the CRM has an 
original maturity of le ss than one year, the CR M is not recognized for capital purposes. 
Collaterals with maturity mismatches are only recognized when their(CRM) original 
maturities are greater than or equal to one year. As a result, the maturity of collat eral 
for exposures with original maturities of less than one year must be matched to be 
recognized. In cases of maturity mismatches, partial recognition shall be given to the 
CRM for regulatory capital as per the formula specified in the New Accord. How ever, in 
all cases, collat eral with maturity misma tches will no longer be recognized when they 
have a residual maturity of three months or less.  
 
8.2. The maturity of the underlying expos ure and the maturity of the collateral shall be 
defined conservatively. The effective maturity of the underlying should be gauged as the 
longest possible remaining time before the counterparty is scheduled to fulfill its 
obligation, taking into account any applicable grace period. For the collateral, embedded 
options, which may reduce the term of the co llateral, shall be taken into account, so 
that the shortest possible effective maturity is used. 
 
8.3. In case of loans collateralized b y the bank’s own deposits,  even if the tenor of such 
deposits is less than three months or deposits have maturity mismatch vis-à -vis the tenor 
of the loan, the provisions of paragraph 10.1 regarding  de-recognition of collateral 
would not be attracted provided an explicit consent o f the depositor has been obtained 
for adjusting the maturity proceeds of such deposits against the outstanding loan or for 
renewal of such deposits till the full repayment of the underlying loan.

1. Preamble 
 
1.1 Real Estate investment has unimaginable upsid e potential in boom period and equally 
disastrous down side risks in economic down turns. The en ormity and rapidity of u pside 
potential attracts an investor.  Akin to capital market, the credit risk in exposures to Real 
Estate has brought to naught many a f inancial institutions.  The need and desirability to fix 
limits carefully on exposures, stringe nt margin stipulations, cautious counter party due-
diligence, conservative valuation guidelines, strict review requirements, zero-tolerance to 
any compliance issue, etc. are self-evident.  
 
1.2 Bank formulated the separate Policy on Real Esta te Sector in June 2006 as per RBI 
communication dated 29th June, 2005 which indicated that as exposure of the Banks to the  
Real Estate Sector, particularly to the land developers and builders are on the rise, a 
corresponding control mechanism for managing the risks involved in this sensitive secto r.  
Which suggested, Banks to put in place the following system for managing the portfolio :  
 
1.2.1 Banks should have a Board mandated policy in respect of their real estate exposure. 
1.2.2 The Policy to include exposure limi ts, collaterals to be considered, margins to be kept, 
sanctioning authority / level, sector to be financed, etc. 
1.2.3 Banks should have risk management system in place for containing r isks involved in th e 
sector, including price risk, etc. 
1.2.4 Bank should have a mo nitoring mechanism to ensure that the poli cy stipulation is being 
followed by field functionaries and that their exposure to this sensitive secto r is within the 
stipulated limit.   
1.2.5 The above instructions are indicative in nature and it is left to the individual Banks to adopt 
an appropriate system depending upon the portfolio size, business complexities, risk 
appetite, etc.  
 
1.3 The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 w as passed by the Rajya Sabha on

5. Loan-To-Value Ratio (ltv): 
 
5.1 Realty exposure needs to recognize the credit risk in a discer nible manner through 
appropriate Risk Measures.  The Real Estate property is susceptible to very volatile price  
movements either way and bank lending must, witho ut choice, take into account downside 
risk of property prices and the consequential credit defaults. Risk in encashment of security 
is a peculiar risk that manifests only during economic downturn.  In this cont ext, Loan-to-
Value Ratio (LTV) is an important R isk measurement tool. The LTV is the loan amount 
expressed as a percent of the appraised / accepted value of the property.  If the property is 
valued at Rs.1.00 lakh and the loan amount is Rs.0.80 la kh, the LTV is 80% (Rs.8000 0/- loan 
amount divided by t he Rs.1.00 lakh purchase price).  From the Bank's stand point, a high 
LTV is more risky and the low LTV is higher safety.

1. Overview 
 
1.1 Bank credit extended to registered Non-Banking Finance Companies-Micro Finance Institutions

Self Regulatory Organization (SRO) for the sector for on lending to individuals and m embers

1.2 As per latest RBI Master Directions RBI/DOR/2021-22/89 DoR.FIN.REC.95/ 03.10.038 /2021 -22 
March 14, 2022, (Updated as on July 25, 2022), a micro finance loan is defined as a collateral 
free loan given to a household having annual income up to Rs 3.00 lakhs. For this purpo se, 
household shall mean an individual family unit i.e husband wife, and their unmarrie d 
children. 
 
1.2.1 All collateral-free loans, irrespective of end use and mode of application/processing /

i.e., households having annual income upto Rs.3,00,000 shall be considered as microfinance

Annexure VII to Loan Policy 
Guidelines on Financing to Asset Reconstruction 
Company 
1. Introduction  
 
1.1 Asset Reconstruction Company (ARC) is a financial institution that acquires the Non-Performing 
Assets (NPAs) or bad assets from Banks and Financial Institutions.  
 
1.2 In the Budget for 2021-2022, the Asset Reconstruction Company (ARC) was proposed to be set-
up by the state owned and private sector Banks. The ARC shall have an Asset Ma nagement 
Company (AMC) to manage and sell the NPAs/ Bad assets.  
 
1.3 The Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest 
(SARFAESI) Act, 2002 provides the legal basis for the setting up of ARCs in India . The SARFAESI 
Act assists in reconstruction of bad assets without the intervention of courts.  
 
1.4 The Reserve Bank of India vide ref no. RBI/ DOR/ 2024-25/116 DoR.FIN.REC.16/26.03.001 / 
2024-25 dated 24.04.2024 (updated on 21.01.2025) has issued the regulatory guidel ines 
through the master directions for Asset Reconstruction Companies. The regulatory guid elines 
state that the ARCs play a critical role in the resolution of stressed financial ass ets of banks 
and financial institutions, thereby enhancing the overall health of the financial syst em. To 
ensure prudent and efficient functioning of ARCs and to protect the interest of in vestors, the 
master directions are issued by RBI.  
 
2. Definitions 
 
The important regulatory definitions for the ARC ecosystem are as under:  
 
2.1 “Breakup value” means the equit y capital and reserves as reduced by intangible assets and 
revaluation reserves, divided by the number of equity shares of the investee company. 
 
2.2 “Change in management” means effecting change by the borrower at the instance of ARC in the 
person who has responsibility for the whole or substantially whole of the managem ent of the 
business of the borrower and/ or other relevant personnel. 
 
2.3 “Date of acquisition” means the date on which the ownership of financ ial assets is acquired by 
ARC either on its own books or directly in the books of the trust. 
 
2.4 “Deposit” means deposit as defined in the Companies ( Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014 
framed under Section 73 of the Companies Act, 2013.

PAGE 251

          Page 202 of 299 
 
2.5 “Earning value” means the value of an equity share computed by taking the average of profits 
after tax as reduced by the preference dividend and adjusted for extra-ordi nary and non-

Policy Guidelines on Project Finance 
 
 
1. Introduction  
 
1.1 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has put in place a principle-based comprehensive fram ework 
for early recognition and resolution of stress in borrower accounts on 07.06.2019 referred as 
‘Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets’. In compliance, Bank has also put in 
place board approved policy on resolution of stressed assets.  
 
1.2 The restructuring of exposures relating to projects under implementation on account of 
change in Date of Commencement of Commercial Operations (DCCO) was excluded from the 
ambit of the Prudential Framework.  
 
1.3 Based on a comprehensive review of the regulatory norms, the RBI has rationalized and 
harmonized the extant guidelines by issuing the directions for Project Finance referred as 
‘Reserve Bank of India (Project Finance) Directions, 2025 issued vide ref. no. RBI/ 2025-26/59 
DOR.STR.REC.34/21.04.048/2025-26 dated 19.06.2025. The directions of the RBI shall be 
effective from 01 st October 2025. In compliance with the regulatory directions the policy 
guidelines and operational guidelines on project finance are enumerated in this document.  
 
1.4 The guidelines shall not apply to projects where financial closure has been achieved as on the 
effective date i.e. 01.10.2025. Such projects shall continue to be guided by the existing 
prudential guidelines on project finance, which otherwise shall be treated as repealed. 
However, any resolution of a fresh credit event and/or change in material terms an d 
conditions in the loan contract in such projects, subsequent to the effective dat e, shall be as 
per the guidelines contained in this policy document. 
 
1.5 Resolution of stress in loans not qualifying the definition of ‘project finance’ as sp ecified in 
this policy document, or where the projects are in operational phase, shall co ntinue to be 
guided by the guidelines contained in Prudential Framework or the relevant instructions  as 
applicable.

3. General Guidelines 
 
3.1 Phases of Projects 
 
For Prudential guidelines, the projects shall be broadly divided into three phases as under:  
 
i. Design phase  – This is the first phase which starts with the genesis of the project and 
includes, inter-alia, designing, planning, obtaining all applicable clearances/approvals  till its 
financial closure. 
 
ii. Construction phase – This is the second phase which begins after the financial closure and 
ends on the day before the actual DCCO. 
 
iii. Operational Phase – This is the last phase which starts with commencement of commercial 
operation by the project on the day of the actual DCCO and ends with full repa yment of the 
project finance exposure.

3.2.1 The operational guidelines for sanction of project finance exposures inter alia in complia nce 
with the regulatory guidelines are separately enumerated in operational guidelines on project 
finance.

i. Financial closure has been achieved and original DCCO is clearly spelt out and documented  
prior to disbursement of funds.

included in the loan agreement.

4. Prudential Norms for Resolution 
 
4.1 Resolution of Stress 
 
4.1.1 Bank shall monitor the performance of the project and any buildup of stress on an ong oing 
basis and shall be expected to initiate a resolution plan well in advance. Occurr ence of a 
credit event with any of the lenders during the construction phase, shall trigger a c ollective 
resolution in terms of the Prudential Framework. The reference to ‘default’ in the Prudential 
Framework shall be read as ‘credit event’ for the purpose of project finance accounts, unless 
specified otherwise.

Credit (CRILC) by the lender in the prescribed weekly as well as the CRILC- Main report in

lending arrangement shall also report occurrence of such credit event to all other members of 
the consortium/multiple lending arrangement. The instructions on CRILC report ing shall be 
issued in due course by RBI.

date of such credit event (“Review Period”). The conduct of the lender(s) during thi s Review

resolution plan, wherever required, shall be guided by the provisions of the Prudential 
Framework, unless specified otherwise in this policy guidelines.

Annexure IX to Loan Policy 
 
Policy Guidelines on Gold Loan 
 
 
1. Introduction  
 
1.1 Gold Loan is one the most secured and quickest way of financing. Lending under t his segment 
is against highly tangible and liquid security of Gold Jewellery and Ornaments.  
 
1.2 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has permitted the Banks to lend against the c ollateral 
security of gold jewellery, ornaments and coins for meeting the short-term financing needs of 
borrowers.  
 
1.3 Prudential and conduct related regulations for gold loans have been issued by RBI from t ime 
to time. The extant regulatory regulations are guided, inter alia, by the o bjective of 
providing the borrowers an avenue to tide over their tight liquidity conditions by leveraging 
the gold jewellery, ornaments or coins that are kept idle, while simultane ously addressing 
the risks for the lenders. In compliance with regulatory guidelines, Bank has put  in place 
comprehensive policy guidelines on gold loan.  
 
1.4 The Reserve Bank of India vide ref no. RBI/2025-26/47 DOR. CRE. REC. 26/21.01.023/2025-26 
dated 06.06.2025 has issued revised directions on lending against Gold Collateral. Th e 
directions are issued as part of moving towards a more principle-based and harmonise d 
regulatory framework and addressing possible prudential and conduct related gaps. The 
revised policy and operational guidelines on loan against gold collateral on review are in 
compliance with regulatory guidelines.  
 
2. Applicability and Scope of the Directions 
 
2.1 The effective date of applicability of the revised guidelines shall be 01st April 2026. 
 
2.2 The existing loans sanctioned prior to the effective date shall be governed by the  extant 
guidelines and regulations. The revised guidelines shall also be applicable for the existing 
loans during renewal of the gold loan.  
 
2.3 These guidelines shall be applicable to all loans offered by the Bank for the pu rpose of 
consumption or income generation (including farm credit) where eligible gold is accepted as a 
collateral security.

3. Definitions  
 
3.1 Bullet Repayment Loans means loans where both principal and interest are due for payment 
at the maturity of the loan. 
 
3.2 Collateral Security  or Collateral means an existing asset of the borrower pledged to the 
lender for availing and securing a credit facility extended by the lender to the borrower. 
 
3.3 Consumption Loan means any permissible loan that does not fit the definition of income 
generating loan. 
 
3.4 Eligible Collateral means the collateral of jewellery, ornaments or coins made of gold. 
 
3.5 Loan to Value (LTV) ratio on a day means the ratio of the outstanding loan amount to the 
value of the pledged eligible collateral as on that day. In case of bullet repay ment loans, 
however, the LTV calculation shall take into account the total amount repayable at maturity. 
 
3.6 Income Generating Loan means loans extended for the purpose of productive economic 
activities, such as farm credit, loans for business or commercial purposes, loans for creation 
or acquisition of productive assets etc. 
 
3.7 Jewellery means items that are designed to be worn as personal adornments. 
 
3.8 Ornaments means items meant for use as adornment of any object, decorative items, or 
utensils, excluding those items that fall under the definition of jewellery as defined above i n 
point no. 3.7 above.  
 
3.9 Primary Gold means gold in any form other than in the form of a jewellery, ornaments and 
coins. 
 
3.10 Top-up Loan means an additional loan sanctioned over and above an outstanding loan, during 
the tenor of the original loan, based on the strength of the collateral already pled ged for the 
existing loan.

10. Collateral Management 
 
A. Handling and Storage of Collateral 
 
10.1 Necessary infrastructure and facilities should be in place and appropriate security measures 
undertaken taken in each of the branches where loans are sanctioned against gold collateral.  
 
10.2 The gold collateral should be handled only in branches of the Bank and only by Bank’s 
employees. 
 
10.3 The collateral should b e stored only in Bank’s branches manned by Bank’s employees. The 
safe deposit vaults must be fit for storing gold. Loans shall not be extended by branches that 
do not have appropriate secured facility for storage of the pledged eligible collateral. 
 
10.4 The pl edged eligible collateral shall be transported from one branch to another branch in 
case of shifting or closure of branch(es) or exceptional reasons. Shifting of gold collateral in 
case of any exceptional reasons (other than shifting or closure of branches ) shall be 
undertaken with the specific approval of Head, Gold Loan Vertical. 
 
Further, wherever in case any Branch does not have infrastructure facilities like Strong Room, 
Staff, Security, Safe for storage of the eligible collateral etc. the same shoul d be provided 
immediately. Wherever feasible, the Zonal Head may permit shifting the Gold Loan Portfo lio 
of the branch to a nearby branch, upon the recommendation of Regional Head.  Zonal Head 
shall review at quarterly intervals the adequacy of systems for st orage of the eligible 
collateral. 
 
10.5 The periodical review of the adequacy of systems for storage of the eligible colla teral shall 
be undertaken, training shall be provided to the staff concerned and internal audit of all 
procedures shall be undertaken to ensure that the guidelines are strictly adhered to.  
 
10.6 As part of internal audit, periodic surprise verification shall be carried out for the gold 
collateral pledged and a record thereof to be maintained. A clause in the  loan agreement is 
incorporated for obt aining consent of the borrower(s) to carry out surprise verification 
including assay of the pledged eligible collateral even in their absence during the tenor of the 
loan. This aspect shall be specifically communicated to the borrower at the t ime of 
sanctioning the loan.

Guidelines ON DIGITAL LENDING 
 
1. Introduction  
 
1.1 Digital Lending involves lending through web platforms or mobile apps, utilizing techno logy 
for authentication and credit evaluation. Lending is always about trying to get  a strategic 
edge. Digital lending involves cust omer onboarding, risk assessment, loan underwriting, 
disbursement and repayment digitally. Digital lending reduces operational costs and 
enhances customer experience. With services such as Video-KYC, Aadhar-based K YC, 
websites and applications with cutting-edge functionalities, loan applica tion procedures will 
become more efficient and less cumbersome. Digital lending will improve the traditio nal 
underwriting procedure with drastic transformation. 
 
1.2 Digital Lending is increasingly utilizing cutting-edge tech nologies such as Artificial 
Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML) and big data analytics to collect and evaluate data 
from multiple sources in order to evaluate the creditworthiness of an applicant more qu ickly 
and efficiently. It is enabling alternative credit scoring which will enable us to extend credit 
to a greater number of individuals, thereby advancing the cause of financial inclusion. 
 
1.3 With the introduction of Digital lending, Banks are promoting paperless lending which has 
given a new path to th e lending ecosystem in India. Banks have adopted the updated 
technology to offer financial services to facilitate ease in lending activity. 
 
1.4 In the near future, technology will continue to disrupt the digital lending ecosy stem, with a 
renewed emphasis on delivering an improved end-to-end customer experience. 
 
2. Scope of the Guidelines on Digital Lending   
 
2.1 The “Guidelines on Digital Lending” codifies the policy and the procedure involved in digital 
lending. The guidelines have been framed after considering va rious developments in the 
digital lending ecosystem. 
 
2.2 The guidelines have been made in compliance with all extant statutory & regu latory 
guidelines issued till date. The guidelines enumerated are applicable for all domestic 
branches/offices and its operations. 
 
2.3 The guidelines will support the Digital framework for introducing emergence of new 
technologies such as AI, ML, 5G, Block chain, etc with our Bank. 
 
2.4 The guidelines cover all the Digital lending Aspects of Customer Acquisition, Customer 
Retention, Customer Engagement, Customer Ease & Convenience, Grievance Handling, etc.

3. Business Rules Engine (BRE) 
Business Rules Engine (BRE) is an application that manages decision processes using pre -
defined logic to define the eligibility checks and/or final approval for a custom er availing 
that loan product/opening an account with the bank. BREs enable precise decision making, 
and are especially useful for complex dependencies, as well as in instances where regulatory 
or organizational rules may require frequent logic chan ges. Depending on the nature of the 
BRE, the BRE can be used to make Digital verifications and take financial decisio ns, which 
are otherwise done traditionally. 
 
Business rule Engines (BREs) are mainly used for the following processes: 
 
a. Preapproval or Preq ualification: To determine customer base for pre-approved Digital 
Lending products. 
b. Eligibility checks: To determine the eligibility of customers at the ap plication stage for 
Digital lending Products which are not pre-approved or pre-qualified.

completing digital & financial due diligence of the customer. 
e. Limit enhancement: To determine limit enhancements for already sanctioned loans.

6.4 Guidelines on Default Loss Guarantee in Digital Lending 
 
1) The guidelines are applicable to DL G arrangements entered under ‘Digital Lending’ 
mechanism.  
 
2) Default Loss Guarantee (DLG) : A contractual arrangement, called by whatever name, 
between the Bank and an entity meeting the criteria laid down at point 3 of the guidelines, 
under which the la tter guarantees to compensate the Bank, loss due to default up to a 
certain percentage of the loan portfolio of the Bank, specified upfront. Any oth er implicit 
guarantee of similar nature linked to the performance of the loan portfolio of t he RE and 
specified upfront, shall also be covered under the definition of DLG.  
 
3) Eligibility as DLG Provider : 
 
Bank may enter into DLG arrangements only with a Lending Service Provide r (LSP)/ other 
Regulated Entity (RE) with which it has entered into an outsourcing (LSP) ar rangement. 
Further, the LSP providing DLG must be incorporated as a company under the Companies 
Act, 2013  
 
4) Structure of DLG Arrangements: DLG arrangements must be backed by an explicit legally 
enforceable contract between the Bank and the DLG provider. Su ch contract, among other 
things, must contain the following details:  
 
a. Extent of DLG cover  
b. Form in which DLG cover is to be maintained with the Bank 
c. Timeline for DLG invocation  
d. Disclosure requirements  
 
5) Forms of DLG: Bank shall accept DLG only in one or more of the following forms:  
 
a. Cash deposited with the Bank 
b. Fixed Deposits maintained with a Scheduled Commercial Bank with a lien marked in favour 
of the Bank 
c. Bank Guarantee in favour of the Bank 
 
6) Cap on DLG: Bank shall ensure that total amount of DLG cover on any outstanding portfolio 
which is specified upfront shall not exceed five per cent of the amount o f that loan 
portfolio. In case of implicit guarantee arrangements, the DLG Provider shall not bear 
performance risk of more than the equivalent amount of five per cent of the underlying loan 
portfolio.  
 
7) Recognition of NPA : Recognition of individual loan assets in the portfolio as NPA and 
consequent provisioning shall be the responsibility of the Bank as per the extant  asset

level. The amount of DLG invoked shall not be set off against the underlying ind ividual

realised, can be shared with the DLG provider in terms of the contractual arrangement.  
 
8) Treatment of DLG for regulatory capital : Capital computation, i.e., computation of 
exposure and application of Credit Risk Mitigation benefits on individual loan assets in the 
portfolio shall continue to be governed by the extant norms  
 
9) Invocation of DLG: The Bank shall invoke DLG within a maximum overdue period of 120

10) Tenor of DLG: The period for which the DLG agreement will remain in force shall not be

Annexure XIII to Loan Policy 
Guidelines on Pre-Sanctioned Credit Lines through 
Unified Payments Interface 
1. Introduction 
 
1.1 In the monetary policy meeting dated 06.04.2023 , the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has 
approved the operation of p re-sanctioned credit lines at Bank s through Unified Payment 
Interface (UPI). This facility assists the citizens to avail and utilize the low ticket but 
high-volume retail loans that will boost the consumption and livelihood in the country.  
 
1.2 A Pre-sanctioned credit line on Unified Payment Interface (UPI) allows the individual to 
access the pre-approved credit, with prior consent, directly through UPI platform thereby 
enabling seamless transactions and immediate access to funds. The credit line is  linked 
to the individual’s UPI ID and can be  used as a funding account.  In other words, a credit 
line is a type of loan that provides the customer with a pr edetermined amount of money 
that can be access ed any time with the facility to withdraw funds multiple times as 
needed. Unlike traditional pers onal loans, where the customer receives a lump sum 
upfront and repay it over time, a credit line allows to withdr aw funds whenever 
required, up to the approved limit. 
 
2. Regulatory Guidelines  
 
2.1 Reserve Bank of India vide their notification no: RBI/2023- 24/58 CO.DPSS.POLC.No.S-
567/02-23-001/2023-2024 dated 04.09.2023 has expand ed the scope of UPI by enabling 
transfer to/from pre-sanctioned credit line at bank s. RBI in its notification has specified 
that Banks may, as per their Board approved policy, stipulate terms and conditions for 
use of Pre-Sanctioned credit lines. The terms may include among other items, credit  
limit, period of credit, rate of interest etc.  
 
2.2 Further, National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has communicated the guidelines 
on Credit L ine through UPI vide th eir operating circular number NPCI/UPI/OC No: 
171/2023-24 dt 20.09.2023 covering all the operational points to be followed.  
 
3. Credit Line on UPI 
 
3.1 Currently Savings account, Overdraft account, prepaid wallets and RuPay Credit Ca rds 
can be linked to UPI. With the introduction of Credit line on UPI, users will be able to add 
pre-sanctioned credit lines issued by the Bank for transactions through the UPI System. 
The key design principles for credit line on UPI are as follows:

i. It is a pre-sanctioned credit line to an individual with prior consent to enabl e 
transactions using the UPI system.  
ii. Transactions will work on the UPI market infrastructure as per UPI procedural 
guidelines.  
iii. Transaction will be authenticated using UPI authentication mechanisms.  
iv. Amount will be debited real time from customer’s Credit account through UPI.  
v. UPI settlement process will be followed, NPCI will provide separate Org Id, a nd hence 
separate settlement reports will be provided to the UPI Credit issuers.  
 
3.2 It is an innovative financial offering designed to revolutionize the lending landscape. This 
facility shall empower in dividuals to access pre-sanctioned credit lines from lenders. It 
facilitates the availability of low-ticket, high-volume retail loans, fostering economic 
growth and enhancing financial inclusion.  For credit line products (like KCC, SOD-FDR 
etc.), customer will use UPI as an additional channel to enable the payment through the 
credit line linked accounts. 
 
3.3 This shall provide a seamless, UPI enabl ed credit lifestyle experience to the customers. 
Customers shall benefit from the ease and the increased opportun ity to use their credit 
lines. Merchant shall benefit from the increase in consumption by being part of credi t 
ecosystem with acceptance of credit lines using QR codes and other payment acceptance 
methods. UPI has become the most preferred payment method i n the recent times. 
Enablement of Credit line through UPI may have huge potential for the growth of the  
credit portfolio of the Bank. Linking of credit line on UPI will provide an assurance to the 
customer for safe and secure transactions. 
 
4. Objective 
 
The objective of Credit Line is to provide additional channel to the customer to ut ilize 
the related merchant payments through UPI in a safe, secur e and faster way. Credit line 
is an extension of the credit card to facilitate payment through running loan ac counts or 
other credit line products.

i. Discovery and linking of Credit Line accounts

v. Dispute Management

on UPI using their Aadhaar Authentication or debit card issued to the credi t facility.

Pre-Sanctioned Credit Lines (revolving/ non-revolving) can be linked to UPI.

Guidelines on Lending to Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) 
and Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) 
 
 
1. Introduction  
 
1.1 The Loan Policy of the Bank, inter-alia lays down the guidelines in respect  of lending to 
Infrastructure Investment Trusts. An Infrastructure investment trust (InvIT) is a trust formed 
under the Trusts Act and registered under the SEBI Infrastructure Investment Trust  Regulations 
2014. The InvITs provide infrastructure developers a route to monetize their operating assets in 
order to free up capital to undertake the construction of more infrastructure projects. In 
addition, it also enables the investors to invest in operating infrastructure assets to earn stable 
income. Presently, the guidelines are defined only for lending to InvITs.  
 
1.2 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) vide notification n o. RBI/2026- 27/109 DOR.CRE.REC. 
89/07.01.001/2026-27 dated 10.06.2026 has issued the final directions on ‘Lending to the Real 
Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and Lending to Infrastructure Invest ment Trusts (InvITs)’. The 
directions harmonize the existing guidelines in respect of lending to InvITs for parity with 
prudential safeguards for lending to REITs considering the similarity in organisat ion structure 
and risks. The guidelines are also prescribe regulatory ceilings for exposure to REITs.  
 
1.3 The Infrastructure Investment Trust is conceptually similar to the Real Estate  Investment Trust 
(REIT), a REIT owns real estate assets whereas InvIT owns infrastructure assets. 
 
2. Definitions  
 
2.1 ‘InvIT’ or ‘Infrastructure Investment Trust’ shall mean the trust registered as such under the 
Securities and Exchange Board of India (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014. 
 
2.2 ‘InvIT assets’ means assets owned by the InvIT, whether directly or through a [holdco and/  or] 
SPV, and includes all rights, interests and benefits arising from and incidental to ownership of 
such assets; 
 
2.3 ‘Completed and revenue generating project’ means an infrastructure project, which prior to 
the date of its acquisition by, or transfer to, the InvIT, satisfies the following conditions –

the relevant project agreement including concession agreement, power purchase agreement or 
any other agreement of a similar nature entered into in relation to the operation of the project 
or in any agreement entered into with the lenders; 
(ii) the infrastructure project has received all the requisite approvals and certifications fo r 
commencing operations; and 
(iii) the infrastructure project has been generating revenue from operations for a period of not 
less than one year; 
 
2.4 ‘Eligible Infrastructure Project’ means an infrastructure project which, prior to the date of its 
acquisition by, or transfer to, the InvIT, satisfies the following conditions, – 
 
A. For PPP projects,– 
(i) the Infrastructure Project is completed and revenue generating project, or the 
Infrastructure Project, which has achieved commercial operations date and does no t have 
the track record of revenue from operations for a period of not less than one year, or 
    (ii) the Infrastructure Project is a pre-COD project 
 
B. In non-PPP projects, the infrastructure project has received all the requisite approvals  and 
certifications for commencing construction of the project. 
 
2.5 ‘Pre-COD Project’ means an infrastructure project which, – 
 
(i) has not achieved commercial operation date as defined under the relevant project 
agreements including the concession agreement, power purchase agreement or any othe r 
agreement of a similar nature entered into in relation to the operation of a project or any 
agreement entered into with the lenders; and 
 
(ii) has, – 
 
(1) achieved completion of at least fifty per cent of the construction of t he infrastructure 
project as certified by an independent engineer of such project; or

3.5 Security Coverage 
 
3.5.1 Financing to a REIT shall be fully secured inter alia by charge over the unde rlying immovable 
property, an assignment of rental cash flows and receivables, a pledge of equity  interests held

in the nature of an exclusive first charge, or a first pari passu charge where multiple lenders 
are involved, governed by an inter-creditor agreement or any other arrangements amongst such

holds, directly or through one or more intermediate entities, an immovable property.

underlying SPVs from acting to the detriment of the creditors, e.g., restrictions on issu ing

5. Exposure Norms  
Bank shall fix internal limits for the aggregate exposure to real estate sector, a s also sub-limits 
for various sub-categories of real estate exposures. 
The sub-limit for Bank’s aggregate exposure towards Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) shall 
be subject to a prudential ceiling of 10% of the Bank’s eligible capital base.  
 
(The guidelines on exposure norms shall form part of extant credit risk management policy).  
 
6. Risk Weighted Assets  
Exposures to Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) shall be treated as Commercia l Real Estate 
(CRE) exposures and shall attract a risk weight of 100 per cent. However, if such exp osures 
qualify as capital market exposures in terms of paragraph 95A of the Reserve Bank of India 
(Commercial Banks - Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025, the applicable risk  
weight shall be 125 per cent. 
 
Lending to REITs undertaken by overseas branch of the Bank shall attract a risk weight of 150 
per cent. 
 
(The guidelines on exposure norms shall form part of extant credit risk management policy).
